Reading a quote and converting an amount from one currency to another
The same rate can be quoted two ways (reciprocals): e.g. dollars per euro vs euros per dollar
Appreciation (a currency buys more foreign currency, strengthens) vs depreciation (buys less, weakens)

How a stronger/weaker home currency affects exports and imports

claims.claim: An exchange rate is the price of one currency expressed in terms of units of another currency.
A given exchange rate can be quoted two reciprocal ways; when one currency strengthens against another, the other weakens proportionally.
A currency appreciates (strengthens) when its exchange rate rises so it buys more of another currency, and depreciates (weakens) when it buys less.

In a floating system the exchange rate is set by supply and demand for the currency in the foreign exchange market; the U.S. dollar floats, and neither the Treasury nor the Federal Reserve targets a level for it.
A higher interest rate or expected rate of return relative to other countries tends to attract capital and cause a nation's currency to appreciate.
Higher relative inflation erodes a currency's purchasing power and tends to make it depreciate; over the long run exchange rates tend toward purchasing power parity.
Expectations of future appreciation or depreciation affect both demand and supply for a currency, which can make exchange-rate movements self-reinforcing in the short run.
A weaker (depreciated) home currency makes that country's exports cheaper to foreign buyers and makes imports more expensive at home; a stronger currency does the reverse.
Exchange-rate movements affect incentives to export and import and therefore aggregate demand; it is a mistake to label exports simply 'good' and imports 'bad' because exchange rates connect the two.

Regimes range along a spectrum: floating (market-set), soft peg / managed float (market-set with central-bank intervention to smooth movements), hard peg (central bank fixes and defends a value using reserves and monetary policy), and adopting another country's currency (merged currency).
A fixed regime buys exchange-rate certainty but subordinates domestic monetary policy to defending the peg; a floating regime keeps monetary-policy flexibility but allows the rate to fluctuate.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether fixed or floating regimes are 'better'
positions: Fixed reduces currency risk and trading costs, aiding trade
Floating preserves independent monetary policy and lets the rate absorb shocks
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as a genuine tradeoff, not a settled question; the lesson names both sides and does not declare a winner, consistent with the subject's positive-vs-normative caution.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Economics 2e, Section 29.1: How the Foreign Exchange Market Works
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch 2026-08-19. Supports: exchange rate = the price of one currency in units of another; a rate can be quoted reciprocally so that when one currency strengthens the other weakens proportionally (dollar/Canadian-dollar illustration, $1.17 in 1980 appreciating to $1.39 in 1986); appreciation/strengthening vs depreciation/weakening; and the main foreign-exchange participants (trading firms, tourists, foreign direct investors, portfolio investors hedging or speculating). Facts used under CC BY with attribution; prose written original.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Economics 2e, Section 29.2: Demand and Supply Shifts in Foreign Exchange Markets
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch 2026-08-19. Supports: a floating rate moves when demand/supply for the currency shift; a higher relative interest rate or expected rate of return leads a currency to appreciate; expectations of a future rate change affect both demand and supply (self-reinforcing short-run moves); higher relative inflation erodes purchasing power and depreciates a currency (Mexican peso 1986-87 with inflation over 200% falling from $2.50 to $0.50 per peso); and long-run purchasing power parity via arbitrage. Facts used under CC BY with attribution; prose written original.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Economics 2e, Section 29.3: Macroeconomic Effects of Exchange Rates
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch 2026-08-19. Supports: a stronger home currency discourages exports and makes imports cheaper, while a weaker currency encourages exports and makes imports more expensive (French-firm example with the euro moving from $1.06 in 1999 to $1.37 in 2013); exchange-rate movements affect aggregate demand; and the caution that labeling exports 'good' and imports 'bad' overlooks the role of exchange rates. Facts used under CC BY with attribution; prose written original.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Economics 2e, Section 29.4: Exchange Rate Policies
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch 2026-08-19. Supports: floating rates set by market supply and demand (the U.S. dollar; roughly 40% of economies); soft peg = market-set with central-bank intervention to smooth excessive moves; hard peg = central bank fixes and defends a value using reserves/monetary policy; merged currency = adopting another nation's currency (Ecuador using the U.S. dollar); and the tradeoff that a fixed regime gives up independent monetary policy for exchange-rate certainty. Facts used under CC BY with attribution; prose written original.

sourceRecords.title: How does the foreign exchange value of the dollar relate to Federal Reserve policy? (FAQ)
sourceRecords.provider: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch 2026-08-19. Supports: the value of the dollar is determined in foreign exchange markets (a floating currency); the U.S. Treasury is the lead agency on dollar policy; neither the Treasury nor the Federal Reserve targets a level for the exchange rate; and the dollar is an important consideration for monetary policy because it influences U.S. prices and activity. Used to corroborate the floating-regime and interest-rate-link points with a non-OpenStax government source; no prose reproduced.
